subject: literature
passage: The tram lurched, and Fenn, who had been thinking of nothing in particular, which is to say of the Hargreave account and its missing four shillings, caught at the strap and saw in the dark window his own face laid over the passing shops, the face of a man of forty, hat a little crooked. Was that what they saw at the office? Well. A boy across the aisle was eating an orange, peeling it in one long spiral, unhurried, as if the tram and the Hargreave account and all of London could wait, and quite suddenly Fenn was glad, absurdly glad, of the smell of it, sharp and sweet in the damp air, and of the boy, and even of the four shillings, which would turn up, which always turned up.
stem: Based on the text, what prompts Fenn's sudden change of mood?

choices.A: Discovering at last where the four shillings missing from the Hargreave account had gone
choices.B: Arriving at his office after a long and uncomfortable ride through the streets of London
choices.C: Seeing his reflection in the window and deciding that he looks younger than he had feared
choices.D: Watching a boy peel an orange slowly, as though nothing around him required any hurry

explanation.why: Fenn's worries (the account, his tired reflection) give way when he notices a boy peeling an orange "unhurried, as if the tram and the Hargreave account and all of London could wait." Right after this, "quite suddenly Fenn was glad ... of the smell of it ... and of the boy." The boy's calm, unhurried act triggers the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Fenn only expects the shillings to "turn up"; he has not found them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Fenn is still on the tram; the passage never shows him arriving at the office.
explanation.C: Incorrect. His reflection shows "a man of forty, hat a little crooked," and leads him to an uneasy question, not to relief.
explanation.D: Correct. The gladness follows directly from watching the unhurried boy and smelling the orange.
